issues.legal_issue: The presumption of due execution and attestation for an ancient document does not apply to a copy merely because the copy is admitted as secondary evidence.
material_facts: The original will was not produced, and the courts below found that it had been deliberately withheld by the appellants.
A certified copy obtained from the court record of an earlier suit was admitted as secondary evidence of the will’s contents.
The copy was more than thirty years old and came from proper custody.
issues.conclusion: The copy could be admitted as secondary evidence of the will’s contents, but its age and custody did not permit a presumption that the original will had been duly executed and attested.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 65 and 90 of the Evidence Act, a copy may be admitted as secondary evidence where the requirements for secondary evidence are met. The presumption under section 90 as to execution and attestation applies to an original document, not a copy. For a copy admitted under section 65 and produced from proper custody, only the signatures authenticating the copy may be presumed genuine. The Court followed Harihar Prasad v. Must. of Munshi Nath Prasad and relied on Munnalal v. Krishibai and Basant Singh v. Brij Raj.

rule.if: testamentary_validity_dispute and original_will_not_produced and copy_admitted_as_secondary_evidence and copy_more_than_thirty_years_old and copy_from_proper_custody

predicates.testamentary_validity_dispute: The proceeding disputes whether a will is valid.
predicates.original_will_not_produced: The original will is not produced in evidence.
predicates.copy_admitted_as_secondary_evidence: A copy of the will is admitted as secondary evidence of its contents.
predicates.copy_more_than_thirty_years_old: The copy is more than thirty years old.
predicates.copy_from_proper_custody: The copy is produced from proper custody.

issues.definition: When a will is disputed and only an old copy from proper custody is admitted as secondary evidence, the copy does not by itself establish that the original was duly executed and attested.

issues.legal_issue: Due execution, attestation, and the testator’s sound disposing state of mind may be established by evidence independent of the presumption for an ancient original document.
material_facts: The original will was filed in an earlier suit soon after its execution, and the testator’s mother relied on it in claiming the property.
The mother dealt with the property as its absolute owner and executed settlement deeds in favour of her daughters.
An attesting witness testified that the testator executed the will, that he attested it, and that the testator was in a sound disposing state of mind.
The courts below accepted the witness’s identification and testimony, and the terms of the will were found to be natural and rational.
issues.conclusion: The evidence apart from any presumption under section 90 justified finding that the will was executed and attested and that the testator was in a sound disposing state of mind.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the lack of a section 90 presumption did not prevent proof of execution and attestation through other evidence. It relied on the attesting witness’s testimony, the circumstances and conduct surrounding the will, and the rationality of its terms. Setthaya v. Somayajulu was applied in holding that, once a copy is properly admitted as secondary evidence of a document’s terms, the court may construe those terms.

rule.if: testamentary_validity_dispute and execution_contested and attesting_witness_testified and witness_identification_accepted and conduct_supported_will and terms_were_natural_and_rational

predicates.testamentary_validity_dispute: The proceeding disputes the validity of a will.
predicates.execution_contested: A party disputes whether the testator executed the will.
predicates.attesting_witness_testified: A person who attested the will testified about its execution and the testator’s condition.
predicates.witness_identification_accepted: The court accepted that the witness was an attesting witness to the will.
predicates.conduct_supported_will: The testator’s family members acted in ways consistent with treating the will as valid.
predicates.terms_were_natural_and_rational: The court found the will’s terms natural and rational in the circumstances.

issues.definition: In a dispute about a will, accepted testimony from an attesting witness, supported by the parties’ conduct and the rationality of the will’s terms, can establish execution, attestation, and sound disposing state of mind without relying on an ancient-document presumption.

issues.legal_issue: A deceased testator’s statement about his age in a will is relevant to establish the commencement of his relationship by blood.
material_facts: The testator stated in the will that he was nineteen years old when he executed it.
The testator was deceased when the statement was tendered, and the question whether he was a major when he made the will was disputed.
issues.conclusion: The testator’s statement about his age in the will was admissible and could be relied on in deciding whether he was a major.
issues.legal_principle: Section 32(5) of the Evidence Act permits a deceased person’s statement about a relationship by blood where the maker had special means of knowledge. A statement about age can relate to the existence of that relationship because age indicates the commencement of the relationship by blood. The Court relied on Oriental Government Security Life Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Narasimha Chari, Rama Chandra Dutt v. Yogeshwar Narain Deo, Mohammed Syedol Ariffin v. Yeohooi Gark, and the other decisions discussed in its judgment.

rule.if: will_age_dispute and deceased_maker and age_statement_in_will and statement_concerns_makers_own_age

predicates.will_age_dispute: The proceeding disputes whether a testator was of the required age when making a will.
predicates.deceased_maker: The person who made the statement is deceased when it is tendered.
predicates.age_statement_in_will: The statement about age appears in the will.
predicates.statement_concerns_makers_own_age: The statement gives the age of the person who made it.

issues.definition: In a dispute about a testator’s age, the deceased testator’s own statement of age in a will is admissible as evidence relating to the commencement of a blood relationship.

issues.legal_issue: A deceased family member’s statement about age is inadmissible under the relationship-statement provisions when made after an actual controversy on that point has arisen.
material_facts: In an earlier suit, the testator’s mother asserted in her written statement that he was a major after the opposing party had alleged that he was a minor.
The dispute about the testator’s age therefore existed when the mother made the statement.
The statement was relied on in the later proceeding to establish the testator’s age.
issues.conclusion: The mother’s statement in the earlier written statement was inadmissible under sections 32(5) and 32(6) of the Evidence Act because it was made after the controversy had arisen.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 32(5) and 32(6) require the relevant statement to have been made before the question in dispute was raised. This means before any actual controversy concerning the subject matter, not merely before the particular litigation in which the statement is later tendered. The Court relied on Bahadur Singh v. Mohan Singh and Kalka Prasad v. Mathura Prasad.

predicates.relationship_statement_dispute: The proceeding relies on a deceased person’s statement as evidence of a family relationship or related fact.
predicates.deceased_family_declarant: The person who made the statement was a family member and is deceased when the statement is tendered.
predicates.statement_made_after_actual_controversy: The statement was made after an actual controversy about the relevant fact had arisen.

issues.definition: A deceased family member’s statement cannot be used as relationship evidence when it was made after an actual dispute about the relevant fact already existed.

issues.legal_issue: The party relying on a will bears the burden of proving that the testator was a major, and that burden may be discharged by admissible evidence and consistent family conduct.
material_facts: The respondents relied on the will, and the appellants disputed that the testator was a major when it was executed.
The testator’s statement in the will that he was nineteen was admissible.
An attesting witness testified about the will’s execution and the testator’s condition.
The conduct of the family members was consistent with their understanding that the testator was a major and that the will was valid.
The documentary and other oral evidence relied on to show a different age was found unreliable, inadmissible, or speculative.
issues.conclusion: The respondents discharged the burden of proving that the testator was a major when he executed the will.
issues.legal_principle: The burden of proving that a testator was a major when executing a will lies on the party relying on the will. The Court cited Ganaprakasam v. Paraskthy and concluded that the admissible age statement, the attesting witness’s evidence, and the parties’ conduct together established majority.

rule.if: will_age_dispute and party_relies_on_will and admissible_testator_age_statement and supporting_attesting_witness_evidence and family_conduct_consistent_with_majority

predicates.will_age_dispute: The proceeding disputes whether the testator was of the required age when making a will.
predicates.party_relies_on_will: A party relies on the will to establish a right to property.
predicates.admissible_testator_age_statement: The testator made an admissible statement about his age.
predicates.supporting_attesting_witness_evidence: An accepted attesting witness gave evidence supporting the will’s execution and the testator’s condition.
predicates.family_conduct_consistent_with_majority: The family members acted consistently with an understanding that the testator was a major when making the will.

issues.definition: A party relying on a will discharges the burden of proving the testator’s majority when admissible age evidence, supporting witness evidence, and consistent family conduct establish that fact.

issues.legal_issue: An administrative memorandum or endorsement concerning the absence of register entries is not admissible without testimony from its maker and proof of the diligent effort to locate the original register.
material_facts: The appellants produced a memorandum and an endorsement stating that there were no birth-register entries concerning the testator’s family for the relevant year.
Neither document’s writer was examined to testify to its contents.
No evidence established that the original register could not be found despite diligent efforts.
issues.conclusion: The memorandum and endorsement were inadmissible without formal proof of their contents and the efforts to establish that the original registers were untraceable.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the documents could not be admitted without their makers’ testimony to prove their contents and evidence establishing that diligent efforts had failed to locate the original registers.

rule.if: birth_register_evidence_dispute and administrative_record_claims_no_entry and record_writer_not_examined and diligent_search_for_original_not_proved

predicates.birth_register_evidence_dispute: The proceeding disputes a person’s age using evidence about birth-register entries.
predicates.administrative_record_claims_no_entry: An administrative memorandum or endorsement states that no relevant register entry exists.
predicates.record_writer_not_examined: The person who wrote the memorandum or endorsement is not examined to prove its contents.
predicates.diligent_search_for_original_not_proved: The evidence does not establish that diligent efforts failed to locate the original register.

issues.definition: In a dispute relying on an administrative record that reports no register entry, the record is inadmissible if its writer is not examined and a diligent but unsuccessful search for the original register is not proved.

issues.legal_issue: A discrepancy between a will’s general statement that it disposes of the whole estate and its property schedule does not establish partial intestacy when the will expressly manifests an intention to dispose of the whole estate.
material_facts: The body of the will stated that the testator was disposing of all his movable and immovable property in favour of his mother and gave a total land area.
The schedule omitted some survey numbers and its listed measurements did not add up to the total stated in the body.
The discrepancy could have resulted from a mistake in describing survey numbers after changes to the survey records.
issues.conclusion: The testator intended to dispose of his entire property, and the discrepancy did not leave any property undisposed of or create an intestacy.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed the will as a whole and gave effect to its expressly declared intention to dispose of the entire estate. It held that the discrepancy between the body and schedule did not justify an inference that the testator intended to reserve part of his property and leave it intestate.

rule.if: will_construction_dispute and body_expressly_disposes_of_entire_estate and schedule_measurements_discrepant and plausible_description_error

predicates.will_construction_dispute: The proceeding disputes whether a will disposed of all the testator’s property.
predicates.body_expressly_disposes_of_entire_estate: The body of the will expressly states that the testator is disposing of the whole estate.
predicates.schedule_measurements_discrepant: The property schedule omits property or gives measurements inconsistent with the total stated in the body.
predicates.plausible_description_error: The discrepancy may plausibly have resulted from an error in identifying or describing the property.

issues.definition: When a will expressly disposes of the entire estate, a discrepancy in its schedule does not leave property undisposed of if the inconsistency may be a description error.
